title: SVT: vagal manoeuvres and adenosine
stem: A 30-year-old woman has had sudden-onset regular palpitations for 40 minutes. HR 190, BP 112/70, RR 18, SpO2 99%. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no dizziness. Manage her.

phases.title: Assess
phases.goal: Monitoring on; any adverse features? A quick history; read the ECG.

phases.title: Adenosine
phases.goal: Proximal access, warn her, a strip, then adenosine; 12 mg if 6 mg fails.

phases.title: After
phases.goal: A 12-lead in sinus rhythm and bloods; explain, refer, safety-net.

review.text: Adenosine. AHA (Hong Kong ACLS): 6 mg, then 12 mg. RCUK: 6, 12, then 18 mg. The script stops at 12 mg because she converts.
Unstable narrow complex tachycardia. AHA: synchronised 50–100 J. RCUK: 70–120 J. The script only names synchronised cardioversion.

notes:
Checked against RCUK tachycardia algorithm (2021; unchanged 2025), ESC 2019 SVT guidelines and the REVERT trial (Lancet 2015).

Stable regular narrow complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first — the modified Valsalva (REVERT): semi-recumbent, blow into a 10 mL syringe (≈40 mmHg) for 15 seconds, then lie flat with legs raised to 45° for 15 seconds; about 43% convert versus 17% with standard Valsalva. Carotid sinus massage only without bruits or cerebrovascular history (avoid in older patients).

Adenosine: 6 mg rapid IV bolus into a large proximal vein with a 20 mL saline flush, under continuous ECG recording; if unsuccessful 12 mg, then 18 mg (RCUK; AHA uses 6 then 12). Warn the patient about brief chest discomfort, flushing and a sense of doom. Caution in severe asthma (verapamil is an alternative). Reduce the dose (start 3 mg) with dipyridamole, carbamazepine, heart transplant or a central line.

After conversion, look for pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave): WPW needs cardiology referral for ablation, and AV-node blockers must be avoided if she ever presents with pre-excited AF.

Your SVT notes list adult DC cardioversion energies from AHA (100 J for narrow complex); that applies only if unstable.

Perfect script checked against an AHA tachycardia checklist, the RCUK algorithm, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed the wrong options (slow or low-dose adenosine, verapamil). Added: adverse features named, the plan aloud with cardioversion if unstable, bloods, AV-node blockers avoided, and the safety-net. Adenosine follows AHA (6 then 12 mg).

opts.t: Your ECG shows an extra electrical pathway in the heart, called WPW, which causes these fast rhythms. I'll refer you to cardiology for a study and possibly ablation.

qs.q: Why avoid AV-node blockers in pre-excited AF?
qs.a: Conduction speeds down the accessory pathway, risking VF
wrong: They trigger bronchospasm in most patients with WPW
They cause complete heart block in pre-excitation
They are ineffective but otherwise safe to try

qs.a: Short PR, delta wave, broad QRS
wrong: Long PR, narrow QRS, U waves
ST elevation in V1–V3 with RBBB
Peaked T waves and flat P waves

badge.name: Vagus Nerve
badge.flavor: Blow, then legs up. Rapid push, fast flush. Look for the delta wave.

cards.q: Modified Valsalva: after 15 s of strain the patient…
options: Lies flat with legs raised to 45° for 15 s
Sits upright and coughs hard for 15 s
Holds the breath for 60 s while sitting
Drinks iced water while lying on the left side
cards.why: REVERT: the leg raise increases venous return and vagal tone.

cards.q: First adenosine dose for adult SVT?

options: Rapidly into a large proximal vein with a flush
Slowly over 5 minutes through a small hand vein

cards.q: Delta wave is a sign of…
cards.why: Slurred upstroke from early ventricular activation via the accessory pathway.

script.say: Hello Ms Ip, I'm the emergency doctor. Monitoring on, please: ECG, blood pressure and SpO2.
Any chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or fainting?
script.do: None; BP 112/70: no adverse features, she's stable.

script.say: Had this before? Any asthma, heart problems or regular medicines? 12-lead ECG, please.
script.do: Regular narrow complex tachycardia at 190, no P waves.

script.say: She's stable with a regular narrow complex tachycardia, likely SVT: vagal manoeuvres first, then adenosine. If she becomes unstable: synchronised cardioversion under sedation.

Modified Valsalva, with a rhythm strip running. Ms Ip, sitting up at 45 degrees, blow into this syringe hard enough to move the plunger, for 15 seconds; then we'll lie you flat and lift your legs. Now: flat, legs up to 45 degrees for 15 seconds. Look at the strip.
script.do: Back at 45°; strain 15 s; flat with legs raised 15 s; strip: still 190.

script.say: Cannula in the antecubital fossa, with a three-way tap and a 20 mL saline flush.
This medicine stops your heart for a second or two to reset it. You may feel chest tightness, flushing and a sense of doom, but it passes in seconds.
Record a continuous rhythm strip through the push. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push, then flush.
script.do: A two-second pause, then SVT again.

script.say: Adenosine 12 mg rapid IV push, then flush.
12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm: short PR and a delta wave: pre-excitation, WPW. Potassium, magnesium and thyroid function.

Your ECG shows an extra electrical pathway in the heart, called WPW. I'll refer you to cardiology for a study and possibly ablation. Until then, no verapamil or digoxin: with this pathway they can be dangerous.
If it happens again: blow hard for 15 seconds, then lie flat with your legs raised. Come back if it doesn't stop or you feel faint.
